content: Admission to a neonatal intensive care unit, severe hyperbilirubinemia, and cerebral palsy are critical neonatal health concerns. A total of 13 Population, Intervention, Control, and Outcomes (PICO) questions were developed to guide the research and recommendations. The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its recommendations for the prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage. This update builds upon the 2007 WHO recommendations for postpartum hemorrhage prevention and the 2009 WHO guidelines for managing postpartum hemorrhage and retained placenta. The guideline steering group identified additional questions related to postpartum hemorrhage prevention and treatment. These questions were reviewed and prioritized by the guideline development group, incorporating both previously addressed and new questions. The outcomes from the 2007 and 2009 guidelines were adopted, with outcomes rated on a scale from 1 to 9. Outcomes with an average score of 7 or higher were considered critical. WHO staff, in collaboration with external researchers, summarized and appraised the evidence using Cochrane methodology for randomized controlled trials. Evidence summaries for postpartum hemorrhage recommendations were prepared using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to assess the overall quality of evidence. GRADE evaluates study design, study limitations, consistency of results, directness of evidence, and precision of effect estimates. During technical consultations, balance worksheets were used to summarize values, preferences, and judgments regarding the strength of new and revised recommendations. For the WHO guidelines on basic newborn resuscitation, the Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health Department coordinated efforts to review and synthesize evidence on priority questions. The International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation conducted analyses of reviews related to these questions. The WHO process included systematic reviews of relevant literature, preparation of GRADE profiles, and analysis of risks, benefits, values, preferences, and implementation costs. For the guideline on delayed umbilical cord clamping to improve maternal and infant health and nutrition outcomes, the WHO guideline development group discussed evidence, implementation challenges, and research gaps. Ongoing trials were summarized to estimate the magnitude of forthcoming evidence. Systematic reviews and GRADE evidence profiles for critical outcomes were presented during a consultation in February 2013 in Geneva, Switzerland. Research gaps and implementation needs were further discussed in a second consultation in June 2014. Decision-making procedures were established at the start of the meetings, including rules for agreement and documentation. Members of the guideline development group provided additional comments on research gaps and documented their views on the intervention's effects, evidence quality, values, preferences, and costs. The process was enhanced by using an online form for feedback. Two co-chairs with expertise in group processes and evidence interpretation were nominated and approved. WHO Secretariat members facilitated the meeting process but did not vote or have veto power. The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions outlines the preparation and maintenance of Cochrane systematic reviews on healthcare interventions. Five content experts peer-reviewed the draft guideline on delayed umbilical cord clamping. A public call for comments on the final draft was open from August to November 2014. Stakeholders were included in an external review group and could comment after submitting a signed declaration of interests form. Feedback was received from three stakeholders, and WHO staff finalized the guideline for publication. Management of competing interests followed WHO rules. All experts participating in WHO meetings declared relevant interests before participation. Declarations of interest were reviewed by technical officers and relevant departments before finalizing group composition. Participants also verbally declared their interests at the start of each meeting. WHO's conflict of interest rules aim to prevent situations that could compromise the objectivity and independence of experts or the organization. The guideline will be reviewed in 2024. The Department of Nutrition for Health and Development at WHO headquarters will coordinate the update, following formal WHO guideline development procedures. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to evaluate during the next review.
